A business volume becomes a design rate through one chain of real multiplications (events per order, divide by seconds a day, peak ratio, bytes per event, retention, replication) — not a single read of the headline number.

items.item: The peak-to-average ratio is what a system is actually provisioned for; the mean rate is only what it's expected to handle on an average day.

at.step: Reveal: what the peak-to-average ratio actually changes

items.item: Little's Law (L = λW) holds for any stable queueing system and turns a design rate plus a processing time into a real in-flight count.
Dividing the in-flight count by one consumer's own capacity gives the actual number of consumers, connections or queue slots to provision.

items.item: A reference number (a benchmark, a request limit, a measured rate) is only useful paired with what it is not — a planning figure, a hard ceiling, or a vendor claim, respectively.

at.step: Reveal: three reference numbers, each with its own ceiling named

items.item: The same benchmark number can support a narrow, correct claim (one partition won't bottleneck a far lower design rate) while failing to support a broad, incorrect one (this cluster will hit that rate).

at.step: Reveal: using a reference number correctly, and incorrectly

items.item: A warehouse scan rate belongs in the reference-numbers table only as a real, run measurement with its own hardware disclosed — never as a quoted vendor figure.

Little's Law's generality (it holds regardless of the arrival or service distribution, given stability) is why one formula sizes queues, pools and in-flight buffers alike, without a different derivation for each.

This topic fixes the shop's own planning constants (orders a day, events an order, peak ratio, bytes an event, replication, retention) that every later design topic in this chapter imports as its starting numbers.
Provisioning directly off a blog post's benchmark number, without naming what it is not, is this topic's own named production failure mode.
